summary: DAY structural pass maps every b03 company into explicit 2036 need→constraint→technology→company chains. The batch spans semiconductor test, factory/vehicle/delivery autonomy, grid equipment/labor, generation and advanced nuclear. Most chains are presently evidenced; SERV/AUR/SMR remain high-uncertainty commercialization cases but future falsifiers are documented rather than automatically treated as current blockers.

materialFindings.chain: AI compute growth → more complex semiconductor qualification/test intensity → automated test equipment → TER
materialFindings.successorBottleneck: test parallelism, advanced packaging and customer insourcing
materialFindings.falsifier: test intensity per compute dollar structurally falls despite chip complexity

materialFindings.chain: labor/productivity pressure → factory automation/digital control → industrial automation stack → ROK
materialFindings.successorBottleneck: brownfield integration, OT cybersecurity, capex cycles
materialFindings.falsifier: open/vendor-neutral control architectures commoditize incumbent automation economics

materialFindings.chain: road safety/driver labor → ADAS/autonomy → perception/mapping/compute → MBLY
materialFindings.falsifier: OEMs broadly internalize stacks or camera-centric economics fail at higher autonomy

materialFindings.chain: last-mile labor/cost → sidewalk autonomy → small delivery robots/fleet orchestration → SERV
materialFindings.falsifier: dense-market delivery cost per order fails to beat human alternatives at scale

materialFindings.chain: truck-driver scarcity/safety → highway autonomy → driverless trucking stack → AUR
materialFindings.successorBottleneck: certification, terminal network, hardware cost and liability
materialFindings.falsifier: commercial driverless miles fail to improve unit economics or safety case at scale

materialFindings.chain: electrification + AI load → power-quality/distribution bottleneck → switchgear/electrical management → ETN
materialFindings.falsifier: electrical backlog/order growth decouples from load growth for multiple cycles

materialFindings.chain: grid expansion/rebuild → skilled transmission/distribution construction bottleneck → engineering/construction workforce → PWR
materialFindings.falsifier: utility capex rises without sustained outsourced infrastructure demand

materialFindings.chain: high-density industrial/data-center power → medium-voltage distribution/control → engineered electrical systems → POWL
materialFindings.falsifier: record backlog fails to convert while cancellations or margin erosion become structural

materialFindings.chain: 24/7 data-center/electrification load → firm clean generation scarcity → nuclear + dispatchable gas/geothermal portfolio → CEG
materialFindings.successorBottleneck: interconnection, relicensing/restarts, fuel and construction timing
materialFindings.falsifier: long-duration large-load contracts fail to translate into incremental economic value after capex/regulation

materialFindings.chain: large-load reliability → dispatchable/nuclear generation scarcity → diversified competitive generation → VST
materialFindings.falsifier: contracted hyperscaler demand fails to offset commodity/capital intensity across cycle

materialFindings.chain: grid-constrained AI/manufacturing load → behind-the-meter firm power → solid-oxide fuel cells → BE
materialFindings.successorBottleneck: natural-gas availability, interconnect/permitting, manufacturing cost/service durability
materialFindings.falsifier: backlog conversion or service economics deteriorate as competing onsite generation scales

materialFindings.chain: firm low-carbon power need → nuclear construction/scale constraints → modular reactor design/licensing → SMR
materialFindings.successorBottleneck: project financing, customer commitment, supply chain and construction execution
materialFindings.falsifier: approved design fails to achieve binding financed deployment or competitive delivered cost

documentedUnknowns: long-run fuel-cell service durability at hyperscale
binding project financing and delivered cost

contradictions: SMR's regulatory/design first-mover status is real but does not itself establish a financed deployment bottleneck winner; nonbinding TVA/ENTRA1 activity must remain distinct from contracted backlog.
unknowns: Future regulatory timing for autonomy and nuclear remains unknowable and is represented as scenario uncertainty, not fabricated evidence.
peerRequests: Discovery lane: monitor AV certification/regulatory throughput and grid/interconnection constraint migration; red team: attack BE onsite-power substitution and SMR binding-finance assumptions.
